claims.text: Mutation matrix over Prime's control suite: five targeted mutations of attest.py, each run against the UNMODIFIED suite. 7 of 10 controls are OBSERVED FAILING under at least one mutation — human-typed bytes, and-does-NOT-claim, near-miss payload, tampered receipt, tamper blocks attestation, three-receipt setup, and deleted middle receipt. The suite is substantially real, not decorative.

The 3 controls that never failed are NOT shown to be decorative, and saying so would be a false accusation. Two are POSITIVE controls which SHOULD pass under mutations that break negative paths — my matrix contains no happy-path mutation. The third, 'no chain', is a genuine negative control whose NO_CHAIN branch returns early, before any code I mutated. All three are untested by this matrix, which is a gap in my matrix rather than a defect in their suite.

Refinement of CHECKPOINT-04's finding, in Prime's favour. Control #4 DID fail under M3 (attest matching on session alone), so it is not inert in every scenario. But M1 — the verdict literally reading HUMAN_TYPED_ORIGIN_UNRESOLVED — is the exact case it is named for, and it PASSED that. It is a coarse canary that trips when the whole attest path breaks, not the specific check its name promises. The implementation is weaker than the name, not worthless.

MY OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED '6 controls NEVER — DECORATIVE' AND I DID NOT PUBLISH IT. Two mutations had not applied — anchors matched 2x and 0x — and a third crashed before scoring, so six controls were never challenged at all. Absence of failure was absence of a test, and I was one commit away from accusing six of Prime's controls of being decorative on the strength of my own broken mutation anchors.

tests.command: python3 ctl_matrix.py  # 5 mutations of attest.py x unmodified control suite

decisions_requested: Two gaps in MY matrix, offered as the next controls rather than as criticism: no mutation targets the happy path, so the two POSITIVE controls are unexercised; and no mutation reaches the NO_CHAIN early-return, so that control is unexercised. Both are cheap to add and would take the suite from 7/10 proven to 10/10 proven.
risks: M2 produced no score — the suite raised rather than completing — so per-control attribution for that mutation is partial. I counted only what the run printed before it stopped.

A mutation matrix proves a control CAN fail; it does not prove it fails for the RIGHT reason. Control #4 is the example: it failed under M3 while remaining blind to the case it is named for. Counting 'ever failed' as 'discriminating' would repeat exactly that error.
